entries.type: reporting verb — a further statement
entries.patterns: add + that-clause · add + direct quotation · add + noun phrase · add + noun phrase + to + noun phrase · impersonal it should be added that
entries.never: add me that / add someone something / added to me that
notes: Requires something to add to: add cannot open a report. It means "and then this, from the same speaker," so there has to be a then. A paragraph that begins She added that the store was closed sends the reader hunting backward for the sentence it was added to.
entries.meaning: An extra piece appended to what the same speaker just said. Neutral about the content, but it does commit you to the claim that both statements came from one speaker in one stretch of talk.
entries.transform: "It's closed. And the lot is full," he said. -> He said the store was closed and added that the lot was full.
examples: She said the flight was delayed, then added that nobody had told the gate agent.
"And bring a jacket," he added.
The senator added that she would release the full record next week.
He added a line at the bottom of the form and initialed it.
I should add that none of this is official yet.
"We'll be late," she said, and then added, "very late."

entries.type: reporting verb — statement (the inform sense)
entries.register: formal — business, legal, and administrative writing
entries.patterns: advise + sb + that-clause · advise + sb + of + noun phrase · advise + sb + wh-clause · advise + that-clause (impersonal, no listener named) · passive be advised that / be advised of · Please advise. (fixed, standing alone)
entries.never: advise me the total / advise to me
notes: Two different verbs, one spelling: the sense here is "inform." The much commoner sense — "recommend a course of action," advised us to leave early — behaves differently and lives at advise. Only context separates them: He advised me that the road was closed is information; He advised me to take the freeway is a recommendation.
entries.meaning: A formal notification, usually written and usually from an institution. In ordinary American speech it sounds stiff enough to be a small joke — nobody advises a friend that dinner is ready, they tell them.
entries.transform: "Your policy expires on June 1," the letter said. -> The letter advised me that my policy would expire on June 1.
examples: Please be advised that the office will close at noon on Friday.
Counsel advised the court that his client would not testify.
The bank advised us of a change to the account terms.
She advised the committee when the audit would begin.
We will advise you as soon as the shipment leaves the warehouse.
I've attached the invoice. Please advise.

entries.type: reporting verb — public statement
entries.patterns: announce + that-clause · announce + noun phrase · announce + wh-clause · announce + direct quotation · announce + to + sb + that-clause · announce + noun phrase + to + sb · passive it was announced that
entries.never: announce me that / announce us the results / announce about the merger
notes: Word order: this is one of the few verbs here where the to-phrase comfortably precedes the that-clause — announced to the staff that the office was moving is better English than announced that the office was moving to the staff, which briefly says the office is moving to the staff.
entries.meaning: A statement made publicly, formally, or at least to a group. It presupposes an audience, so it sounds oversized for one listener: He announced to me that he was hungry is a joke about self-importance.
entries.transform: "The merger closed this morning," the CEO said. -> The CEO announced that the merger had closed that morning.
examples: The airline announced that all flights out of Denver were canceled.
She announced her resignation in a two-line email.
The school announced to parents that classes would resume Tuesday.
Nobody had announced who was replacing him.
They announced the winners in reverse order.
He walked in and announced that dinner was ruined.

entries.type: reporting verb — a brief remark, often evaluative
entries.patterns: comment + that-clause · comment + on / upon + noun phrase · comment + on + wh-clause · comment + direct quotation · comment + to + sb + that-clause · No comment. (fixed noun use)
entries.never: comment the change / comment me that
entries.meaning: A short opinion offered about something already in view. Unlike remark, which is neutral about content, comment leans slightly toward evaluation — you comment on how something is, not merely that it is.
entries.transform: "The wording is unusually vague," she said. -> She commented that the wording was unusually vague.
examples: He commented that the second draft was much tighter than the first.
Several neighbors commented on the noise.
The mayor declined to comment on the investigation.
"Nice of them to tell us," she commented.
Readers commented under the article for three days.
She commented to a colleague that the numbers looked padded.

entries.type: reporting verb — transmission of a message
entries.patterns: communicate + that-clause · communicate + noun phrase · communicate + noun phrase + to + sb · communicate + to + sb + that-clause · communicate + wh-clause · communicate + with + sb (intransitive — "be in contact") · passive be communicated to sb
entries.never: communicate me the results
entries.meaning: The successful transfer of a message, by any channel — speech, writing, gesture, a look. It is the most abstract verb in this file and the one most likely to be corporate filler: We need to communicate that to the team almost always improves as We need to tell the team.
entries.transform: "The deadline has moved to the 15th," she told the group. -> She communicated to the group that the deadline had moved to the 15th.
examples: The board communicated its decision to shareholders that afternoon.
Somehow he communicated that he was in pain without saying a word.
Please communicate any schedule changes to the front desk.
The two departments barely communicate with each other.
She communicated what the client wanted far more clearly than the brief did.
Nothing about the layoffs was communicated until Friday.

entries.type: reporting verb — resumption after a pause
entries.patterns: continue + direct quotation (usually as an inverted tag) · continue + that-clause (journalistic) · continue + noun phrase · continue + to-infinitive · continue + -ing
entries.never: continue me that
entries.meaning: That the same speaker picked back up after a break — a breath, an interruption, a paragraph. Like add, it cannot start a report, because there has to be something to continue from.
entries.transform: "…and that's the whole story," she said. "Or most of it," she continued. -> She said that was the whole story, then continued that it was really only most of it.
examples: "As I was saying," he continued, "the numbers don't add up."
She paused for a sip of water and continued.
The witness continued that he had never met the defendant before that night.
He continued reading aloud even after everyone had left.
"There's one more thing," she continued, quieter now.
The report continues that no single factor explains the collapse.

entries.type: reporting verb — transmission of content or feeling
entries.patterns: convey + that-clause · convey + noun phrase · convey + noun phrase + to + sb · convey + to + sb + that-clause · convey + wh-clause
entries.never: convey me the message / convey me that
notes: Nearest neighbor: communicate stresses the channel and the act; convey stresses the cargo. You communicate with a colleague; you convey sympathy.
entries.meaning: The getting-across of something, with emphasis on what arrived rather than on the words used. It is the verb of choice for content that was never quite stated: Her tone conveyed that the meeting was over works, while Her tone said that the meeting was over is a metaphor and Her tone told us needs the object.
entries.transform: "Please tell them how sorry I am," he said. -> He asked me to convey his apologies to them.
examples: Her expression conveyed that she had already heard.
Please convey our congratulations to the whole team.
The letter conveyed the board's decision without explaining it.
It's hard to convey how loud the room was.
He conveyed to the family that there was nothing more to be done.
The translation loses almost everything the original conveys.

entries.type: reporting verb — an account of something
entries.patterns: describe + noun phrase · describe + wh-clause · describe + how-clause · describe + noun phrase + to + sb · describe + to + sb + how / wh-clause · describe + noun phrase + as + adjective / noun phrase / -ing
entries.never: describe me the room / describe that the room was dark / describe about the room
entries.meaning: The giving of an account. Note the as-frame, which is where describe does its most useful reporting work: He described the deal as dead attributes the characterization to him and quietly declines to endorse it.
entries.transform: "It was maybe twenty feet long, and gray," she said. -> She described the animal as about twenty feet long and gray.
examples: Can you describe what you saw?
She described the apartment to me over the phone, room by room.
The report describes the response as slow and poorly coordinated.
He described how the machine had failed, one step at a time.
Witnesses described a man in a red jacket.
I don't know how to describe it — you had to be there.

entries.type: verb of talk — names the topic, not the message
entries.patterns: discuss + noun phrase · discuss + wh-clause · discuss + -ing · discuss + noun phrase + with + sb · passive be discussed
entries.never: discuss about the budget / discuss that the budget was tight / discuss me the budget / discuss the budget to me
notes: It reports that talking happened, not what was said. That is why it cannot do reported speech proper: there is no way to convert a quotation into discussed. "The budget is tight," she said becomes She said the budget was tight, never She discussed that the budget was tight. What discuss can report is the subject matter, and the reader is told nothing about who said what or how it came out.
entries.meaning: An exchange of talk on a topic, between two or more people, with no claim about the content, the conclusion, or who held which view.
entries.transform: "Let's go over the budget." — "Fine. Here's where we are." -> They discussed the budget. (Not discussed that the budget was tight — the content is gone.)
examples: We discussed the budget for nearly two hours and settled nothing.
I'd rather discuss this in person.
She discussed the offer with her lawyer before signing anything.
They never discussed what would happen if the funding fell through.
The board discussed moving the deadline to March.
Salaries are not discussed openly here.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement that makes something understood
entries.patterns: explain + that-clause · explain + wh-clause · explain + how/why-clause · explain + noun phrase · explain + to + sb + that-clause · explain + to + sb + wh-clause · explain + noun phrase + to + sb · explain (intransitive) · passive it was explained that
entries.never: explain me something / explain me that / explain me how / explained me to wait
notes: Word order: when both a listener and a that-clause are present, the listener comes first — explained to me that the machine was old. Putting the to-phrase at the end strands it: explained that the machine was old to me reads as though the machine's age belonged to me.
entries.meaning: A statement offered to remove confusion. It presupposes that something needed clearing up, which is why it is not fully interchangeable with say: He said the door was locked is information; He explained that the door was locked implies you had been wondering why you couldn't get in.
entries.transform: "The heater only runs at night," he said. -> He explained to me that the heater only ran at night.
examples: She explained that the deposit wouldn't clear until Monday.
Could you explain the difference to me?
He never explained why he left.
The manual doesn't explain how to reset the timer.
I tried to explain, but nobody was listening.
Let me explain it to you one more time.

entries.type: reporting verb — resumption
entries.patterns: go on + to say / to explain / to add / to argue + that-clause · go on + direct quotation · go on + -ing · go on + about + noun phrase · go on + with + noun phrase
entries.never: go on me
notes: The two -ing / to-infinitive readings are opposites: Frame: went on to say; Means: said the next thing; Example: She finished the summary and went on to say the budget was frozen. // Frame: went on saying; Means: kept saying the same thing; Example: She went on saying the budget was frozen long after it wasn't. // Frame: went on about; Means: talked at tedious length; Example: He went on about the budget for twenty minutes.
entries.meaning: The same speaker moving to the next thing. It is the spoken counterpart of continue and slightly warmer.
entries.transform: "That's the first problem. The second is money," he said. -> He named the first problem and went on to say that the second was money.
examples: He apologized, then went on to explain what had happened.
"Anyway," she went on, "we found the file."
The article goes on to argue that the policy backfired.
She went on talking as if nothing had happened.
Don't get him started — he'll go on about it all night.
Go on, I'm listening.

entries.type: fixed phrase — opinion marker, not a reporting verb
entries.patterns: If you ask me, + clause · clause + , if you ask me · parenthetical inside the clause (The whole thing was, if you ask me, a waste)
entries.never: if you ask to me / if you ask me that
notes: It is not a conditional and it reports nothing: nobody has asked. The phrase flags the clause attached to it as the speaker's own unsolicited opinion, usually one that runs against what everyone else is saying, and it carries a faint note of grievance.
It does not survive being reported. This is the point worth learning: the phrase belongs to whoever is speaking now, so reporting it forces a paraphrase.
entries.meaning: Nothing anyone else said — it marks the attached clause as the speaker's own opinion, offered without being asked. Where say attributes words to someone, this phrase claims them.
entries.transform: "It's too expensive, if you ask me," she said. -> She said that in her opinion it was too expensive. / She said that as far as she was concerned, it was too expensive.
examples: If you ask me, the second album was better.
They repainted the whole thing, which was a waste of money if you ask me.
If you ask me, nobody read the contract before signing it.
He was, if you ask me, never really interested in the job.
That's not a bug, if you ask me — that's a design decision.
If you ask me, they should have canceled the game.

entries.type: reporting verb — an indirect or evidential statement
entries.patterns: indicate + that-clause · indicate + wh-clause · indicate + noun phrase · indicate + to + sb + that-clause
entries.never: indicate me that / indicated to step down
notes: Two jobs at once: with a human subject it reports a statement made indirectly or non-verbally — She indicated that she was willing to settle means she signaled it, not that she announced it. With a non-human subject it reports evidence: The data indicate that costs are rising. The second use is the standard hedge of academic English, and it is deliberately weaker than show or prove.
Number note: in formal American writing data takes a plural verb — the data indicate. In ordinary usage the data indicates is now common and unremarkable.
entries.meaning: A message delivered obliquely, or evidence pointing toward a conclusion. It is deliberately weaker than state and announce: indicate leaves room for the speaker to have meant something else.
entries.transform: "I might be open to an offer," she said. -> She indicated that she might be open to an offer.
examples: The survey indicates that most respondents never opened the email.
He indicated to the committee that he would step down in the spring.
Her silence indicated what she thought of the proposal.
Preliminary results indicate a much smaller effect than expected.
Nothing in the file indicated that the payment had been made.
Please indicate whether you plan to attend.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement delivered to a named listener
entries.patterns: inform + sb · inform + sb + that-clause · inform + sb + of / about + noun phrase · inform + sb + wh-clause · passive be informed that / be informed of
entries.never: inform that the meeting was canceled / inform me the change / inform to me
notes: of vs. about: of is the formal default and takes a fact (informed us of the delay); about is looser and takes a topic (informed us about the new procedure). Neither one can be dropped.
entries.meaning: The formal delivery of information to someone who is entitled to it. It is tell with a suit on, and it carries a faint institutional chill — I regret to inform you is a phrase people brace for.
entries.transform: "Your application was not successful," the email said. -> The email informed me that my application had not been successful.
examples: Nobody informed the neighbors that the water would be shut off.
Please inform your supervisor of any schedule change.
We regret to inform you that the position has been filled.
She was never properly informed about her options.
He informed the officer where he had been that evening.
Keep me informed.

entries.respell: let mee TELL yoo — usually reduced to LEM-ee tell yuh
entries.type: fixed phrase — emphasis marker
entries.patterns: Let me tell you, + clause · clause + , let me tell you · let me tell you + something · let me tell you + about + noun phrase · let me tell you + wh-clause
entries.never: let me to tell you / let me tell to you
notes: It is not a request for permission. Nobody is being asked. The phrase is a pointer that says what comes next matters, and with something attached it usually introduces a complaint or a warning: Let me tell you something — that's not how this works.
It does not survive being reported, for the same reason if you ask me doesn't: the emphasis belongs to the person speaking now. Reporting it means finding a different verb.
entries.meaning: Nothing that was previously said — it announces the speaker's own next statement and marks it as worth hearing. Compare tell, which reports a message that actually reached a listener.
entries.transform: "Let me tell you, that was a long drive," he said. -> He said emphatically that it had been a long drive. / He insisted it had been a long drive.
examples: Let me tell you, that was the coldest I have ever been.
Let me tell you something: nobody reads the second page.
It wasn't cheap, let me tell you.
Let me tell you about the time our flight got canceled in Denver.
And let me tell you why that matters.
Let me tell you, I have never been so glad to see a rest stop.

entries.type: reporting verb — a passing statement
entries.patterns: mention + that-clause · mention + noun phrase · mention + sb (as a topic, never as a listener) · mention + wh-clause · mention + -ing · mention + noun phrase + to + sb · mention + to + sb + that-clause · impersonal it is worth mentioning that
entries.never: mention about the meeting / mention me that
entries.meaning: Something brought up briefly and without emphasis. The word itself is a claim about weight: He mentioned that he was leaving says it came up in passing, and if he actually made a speech about it, mention is the wrong verb. That is also why it works as an apology in advance — I should mention that I'll be late softens the news by pretending it is minor.
entries.transform: "Oh, and I'm out on Friday," she said. -> She mentioned that she would be out on Friday.
examples: He mentioned that his sister lives about an hour from here.
Did anyone mention the parking situation?
She mentioned seeing him at the conference last spring.
I don't think he ever mentioned what he did before this.
Don't mention it to Dave — he'll worry.
It's worth mentioning that the warranty expired in March.

entries.type: reporting verb — a statement of a fact taken as given
entries.patterns: note + that-clause · note + noun phrase · note + wh-clause · note + direct quotation (as a tag) · passive it should be noted that / it is worth noting that
entries.never: note me that
notes: It presupposes truth. This is the one place note is not neutral: He noted that attendance was down takes it as established that attendance was down, and reports him as calling attention to a fact. Compare He claimed that attendance was down, which does the opposite. If the point is contested, note quietly takes a side.
entries.meaning: The act of registering something for the record — observing it, and expecting the reader to accept it.
entries.transform: "Attendance is down about nine percent," the report said. -> The report noted that attendance was down about nine percent.
examples: The judge noted that neither party had filed on time.
It should be noted that these figures exclude part-time employees.
She noted the discrepancy in the margin and moved on.
Critics noted how little had changed since the first audit.
Please note that the building has no visitor parking.
He noted, correctly, that we had no budget for any of this.

entries.type: reporting verb — formal notification
entries.patterns: notify + sb · notify + sb + that-clause · notify + sb + of + noun phrase · notify + sb + of + wh-clause · passive be notified that / be notified of
entries.never: notify that the class was canceled / notify us the date / notify to me / notify us what you decide
entries.meaning: An official act of informing, usually one that some rule or contract requires. It differs from inform in that notify often stands alone with no message at all — Notify the family is a complete instruction, while Inform the family invites the question "of what?"
entries.transform: "You'll hear from us within ten days," they said. -> They said we would be notified within ten days.
examples: The school notified parents that the trip had been canceled.
Tenants must notify the landlord of any change of address.
We were never notified.
Notify the on-call engineer immediately.
She was notified by certified mail on the 12th.
The system notifies you when a payment fails.

entries.type: reporting verb — a considered remark
entries.patterns: observe + that-clause · observe + direct quotation · observe + noun phrase · observe + wh-clause · observe + to + sb + that-clause (literary) · observe + sb + -ing / bare infinitive (the watch sense) · passive it has often been observed that
entries.never: observe me that
notes: Two verbs, and the frames tell them apart: with a that-clause or a quotation it means "said, having noticed" — He observed that the door was open. With a person plus -ing it means "watched" — He observed her leaving. There is no frame where the two readings compete, which is why the ambiguity almost never causes trouble in practice.
entries.meaning: A remark presented as the product of noticing something. Drier and more deliberate than remark, and unlike note it is a spoken act, not a written one.
entries.transform: "Nobody here has read the contract," he said. -> He observed that nobody there had read the contract.
examples: "You're up early," she observed.
He observed that the two accounts contradicted each other on every important point.
One reviewer observed how carefully the film avoids explaining itself.
She observed the whole exchange from across the room.
Visitors may observe the class but may not participate.
It has often been observed that committees expand to fill the time available.

entries.type: reporting verb — attribution of wording
entries.patterns: as + sb + put(s) it · to put it + adverb (bluntly, mildly, simply, another way) · put it + this way / like this / another way · put it + that-clause (formal and rare) · put it + to + sb + that-clause (chiefly British, in questioning)
entries.never: as she put
entries.meaning: The wording, not the fact. As he put it, the project was "resting" attributes the phrasing to him and quietly declines to endorse it — the same move as scare quotes, done with a verb. That is why as he put it so often precedes a euphemism.
entries.transform: "We're pausing the rollout," she said. -> The rollout was, as she put it, "paused."
examples: The building is, as the listing puts it, "full of character."
To put it mildly, the presentation did not go well.
Let me put it another way: there is no money.
He was, as his coach put it, "not a natural."
To put it bluntly, nobody wants the job.
She put it better than I could have.

entries.type: reporting verb — verbatim attribution
entries.patterns: quote + sb · quote + noun phrase · quote + direct quotation · quote + from + noun phrase · quote + sb + as saying / as calling / as describing · quote + sb + on + topic · passive be quoted as saying that…
entries.never: quote that the deal was dead / quoted me that the deal was dead
notes: It is the one verb here that claims exactness. Every other verb in this file reports content; quote reports words. Getting them wrong is not a style problem — misquoting someone is a factual error and, in journalism, a correctable one. Use say or state when you are paraphrasing.
The passive is the workhorse: was quoted as saying is the standard newspaper frame for a statement the reporter did not personally hear.
entries.meaning: Someone's exact words, reproduced. The judgment it carries is a promise of accuracy rather than an opinion about the content — quote says nothing about whether the speaker was right, only that this is what came out of their mouth.
entries.transform: "This deal is dead," he told reporters. -> He was quoted as saying the deal was dead.
examples: The article quotes two former employees who describe the same pattern.
She was quoted as calling the decision "indefensible."
Don't quote me on the exact number.
He quoted his grandmother at least once an hour.
The study is quoted far more often than it is read.
Can I quote you on that?

entries.type: reporting verb — extended narrative
entries.patterns: recount + noun phrase · recount + how-clause · recount + wh-clause · recount + noun phrase + to + sb · recount + to + sb + how-clause
entries.never: recount me the story
notes: Stress matters: /rɪˈkaʊnt/ with second-syllable stress is this verb. /ˈriːkaʊnt/ with first-syllable stress is the election noun — a recount — and the verb meaning "count again."
entries.meaning: The telling of a sequence of events at length and in order. Its object is an episode, not a proposition, which is exactly why the that-clause fits so badly.
entries.transform: "So I got there, and the office was already locked, and…" she said. -> She recounted how she had arrived to find the office already locked.
examples: He recounted the entire trip, hour by hour.
She recounted how the two of them had met.
The memoir recounts his years in Chicago.
Survivors recounted what they had seen to a federal panel.
I've heard him recount that story a dozen times.
The chapter recounts the strike from the union's side.

entries.type: reporting verb — orderly telling
entries.patterns: relate + noun phrase · relate + that-clause · relate + how / wh-clause · relate + noun phrase + to + sb
entries.never: relate me the story
notes: Three unrelated verbs share this spelling, and only the first is a reporting verb: relate a story (tell), relate to something (be connected with — questions relating to the budget), and relate to someone (identify with — I can relate). The third is informal American English and now far more common in speech than the reporting sense, which is why He related the incident sounds distinctly bookish today.
entries.meaning: A full, orderly account given to someone. Slightly more formal than recount and slightly less committed to length.
entries.transform: "It started when the alarm didn't go off," he said. -> He related how the whole day had started with an alarm that didn't go off.
examples: She related the events of that morning to the investigators.
He related that the two companies had been in talks for a year.
The book relates the founding of the town in some detail.
Strange as it may seem, he related the whole thing without once raising his voice.
The witness related what she had heard through the wall.
Ask him to relate the story about the ferry.

entries.type: reporting verb — a brief spoken observation
entries.patterns: remark + that-clause · remark + direct quotation · remark + on / upon + noun phrase · remark + on + wh-clause · remark + to + sb + that-clause
entries.never: he remarked the change / remark me that
entries.meaning: A short, unweighted comment made out loud, often in passing. Compared with its neighbors: observe is more deliberate, comment is more evaluative, note is written and presupposes truth, and remark is the plainest of the four — it reports that something was said aloud and stops there.
entries.transform: "It's colder than it was last week," she said. -> She remarked that it was colder than it had been the week before.
examples: "You've been quiet," he remarked.
She remarked that the parking lot was already half empty at four.
Several people remarked on how much the neighborhood had changed.
He remarked to a friend that he'd never seen the boss so cheerful.
Somebody remarked that the coffee tasted like the pot it came in.
It's rude to remark on what other people are eating.

entries.type: reporting verb — restatement
entries.patterns: repeat + that-clause · repeat + noun phrase · repeat + direct quotation · repeat + wh-clause · repeat + noun phrase + to / for + sb · repeat + oneself
entries.never: repeat me the question
notes: Redundancy watch: repeat again is a double, since repeat already contains the "again." It is common in speech and universally cut in editing. Say repeat or say said it again, not both.
entries.meaning: A statement made a second time, which carries a small implication of insistence or of not having been heard the first time — She repeated that she wasn't going is a stronger sentence than She said again that she wasn't going.
entries.transform: "I'm not signing it. I am not signing it," he said. -> He repeated that he was not going to sign it.
examples: She repeated that the deadline had not moved.
Could you repeat the last part?
He repeated the address back to the dispatcher.
Don't repeat this to anyone.
The recording repeats the same three instructions in a loop.
I'll repeat it for the people in the back.

entries.type: reporting verb — an account given to someone entitled to it
entries.patterns: report + that-clause · report + noun phrase · report + -ing · report + wh-clause · report + to + sb + that-clause · report + sb + as + -ing / adjective · report + on + noun phrase · report + sb + to + sb (denunciation — see below) · passive it was reported that / sb is reported to have
entries.never: report me that / report about the findings
notes: Watch the other senses. Report someone to someone is a denunciation, not a report of speech — She reported him to HR has nothing to do with what he said. And report to plus a person also means "have as a supervisor": He reports to the CFO.
entries.meaning: The passing along of information, and it is scrupulously neutral about truth — the reporter neither endorses the content nor doubts it. That neutrality is the reason it dominates journalism, where claimed would editorialize and revealed would concede the point.
entries.transform: "Sales fell about four percent last quarter," the company said. -> The company reported that sales had fallen about four percent the previous quarter.
examples: Two papers reported that the talks had collapsed.
She reported the outage to the utility just after midnight.
Residents reported hearing a loud bang around two in the morning.
He is reported to have left the country in June.
The committee reported on its findings in November.
Nobody ever reported what happened to the missing equipment.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement (the default)
entries.patterns: say + that-clause · say + direct quotation · say + noun phrase (short fixed list) · say + to + sb (+ that-clause) · say + wh-clause (mostly under negation or a modal: I couldn't say what he meant) · say + to-infinitive with no object (spoken American English only — see the footnote below)
entries.never: say me / say someone something / say me that you're sorry
notes: Pronunciation trap: said rhymes with bed, not with paid, and says rhymes with fez, not with days. The vowel changes even though the spelling doesn't.

say to vs. tell: say to someone is perfectly grammatical, but when a listener is named, tell is far more idiomatic. Reserve say to for when the listener is contrasted or stressed: He didn't say a word to me.

The fixed noun objects: say hello, say goodbye, say yes, say no, say thank you, say grace, say a few words, say nothing, say so, needless to say, say the word, that is to say. None of them needs quotation marks — She said hello is complete as it stands.

The honest footnote: objectless say + to-infinitive — He said to wait. She said not to touch it. — is extremely common in spoken American English and is what most Americans would actually produce. Edited prose still prefers He told us to wait. What is never possible in any register is the personal object: He said me to wait. See Reported commands and requests.
entries.meaning: That words were produced. It is the unmarked, weightless default — the verb you use when you have no reason to use any other, and the one that adds nothing at all to the message.
entries.transform: "I'm not coming," she said. -> She said (that) she wasn't coming. | "I'll call you tomorrow," she said. -> She said she would call me the next day.
examples: He said he'd be here by six.
"That's not what I meant," she said.
She didn't say a word to anyone all afternoon.
What did the doctor say?
The sign says the pool closes at nine.
I couldn't say why he changed his mind.
Just say the word and we'll leave.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement offered to a group
entries.register: neutral, with a workplace and therapeutic flavor
entries.patterns: share + that-clause · share + noun phrase · share + noun phrase + with + sb · share + with + sb + that-clause · share + wh-clause · share (intransitive — Would anyone like to share?)
entries.never: share me the news / share the news to me
notes: Register warning, said plainly: share that has become a soft corporate and therapeutic substitute for tell and say — I wanted to share that we're restructuring. It is completely grammatical, and plenty of readers find it evasive, because it dresses an announcement up as a gift. In neutral prose, tell and say are usually better.
entries.meaning: The offering of information to a person or group, framed as generous or voluntary.
entries.transform: "I've decided to take the job," she told the group. -> She shared with the group that she had decided to take the job.
examples: He shared the news with his family before it went public.
She shared that she'd been out of work for most of the year.
Would anyone like to share before we wrap up?
I'll share the document with you this afternoon.
Nobody shared what had been discussed in the closed session.
Thanks for sharing that with us.

entries.type: reporting verb — a deliberate, on-the-record statement
entries.patterns: state + that-clause · state + noun phrase · state + wh-clause · state + direct quotation · state + to + sb + that-clause · passive it is stated that
entries.never: state me that / state about the delay
notes: The weakness of overuse: in student writing state is often substituted for say to sound serious, and it backfires. My mother stated that dinner was ready is comic. Save it for occasions that genuinely have a record.
entries.meaning: A statement made explicitly and for the record — heavier and more deliberate than say, and neutral about truth in a way claim is not. If someone writes He stated that he was home all evening, they are reporting a formal assertion without commenting on it; He claimed that he was home all evening invites you to doubt it.
entries.transform: "I was at home all evening," he said. -> He stated that he had been at home all evening.
examples: The contract states that either party may cancel with thirty days' notice.
She stated her objection for the record.
Please state your name and occupation.
The memo stated clearly that no exceptions would be made.
He stated to investigators that he had never seen the documents.
It is stated nowhere in the policy that overtime must be pre-approved.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement, command, or information delivered to a named listener
entries.patterns: tell + sb + that-clause · tell + sb + noun phrase (double object) · tell + sb + to-infinitive · tell + sb + wh-clause · tell + sb + about + noun phrase · tell + sb + of + noun phrase (formal) · tell + sb + direct quotation (as a tag) · tell + noun phrase (fixed objects only — see below) · passive be told that / be told to
entries.never: tell that the road was closed / tell to me / "I'm late," he told.
notes: The fixed objects — tell with no listener. A short, closed list where tell takes a non-person object and names nobody: Expression: tell the truth; Example: Just tell the truth. // Expression: tell a lie; Example: He's telling a lie and he knows it. // Expression: tell a story / a joke; Example: She told a story about her first job. // Expression: tell time; Example: He learned to tell time in kindergarten. (British: tell the time) // Expression: tell the difference; Example: I can't tell the difference between the two files. // Expression: tell A from B; Example: Can you tell margarine from butter? // Expression: tell fortunes; Example: Her aunt tells fortunes at the county fair. // Expression: tell tales; Example: Stop telling tales about your brother. // Expression: you never can tell; Example: It might work. You never can tell. // Expression: to tell (you) the truth; Example: To tell you the truth, I forgot.

The other verb: in several of those, tell does not mean "say" at all — it means distinguish or know: I can't tell if it's working. You can tell she's nervous. That sense takes no listener and no message, and it never appears in reported speech.

The passive is everywhere: I was told the office had moved. We were told to wait. Because English promotes the person object, the passive of tell is one of the commonest ways to report a statement whose source you can't or won't name.
entries.meaning: The delivery of a message to a specific person. Where say reports that words existed, tell reports that they reached someone — which is why it, and not say, carries commands: told me to sit down.
entries.transform: "The road is closed," he said to me. -> He told me (that) the road was closed. | "Sit down," she said. -> She told me to sit down.
examples: She told me the meeting had moved to Thursday.
Nobody told us where to park.
He told the kids to stay off the ice.
Tell me about the new place.
I was told the check had already been mailed.
You can tell she's done this before.
To tell you the truth, I'd rather stay home.

entries.type: reporting verb — statement made in writing
entries.patterns: write + that-clause · write + noun phrase · write + direct quotation · write + sb + that-clause (American English) · write + to + sb · write + about + noun phrase · write + wh-clause · write + noun phrase + to + sb · write + saying that…
entries.never: write me to come
notes: American/British split — and here American English is the looser one: Person alone; American: I'll write you next week.; British: I'll write to you next week. // Person + message; American: She wrote me that she'd arrived.; British: She wrote to me to say she'd arrived. // With to; American: Also fine: I'll write to you.; British: Required
entries.meaning: A statement made in writing, which is the only thing separating it from say. Everything about backshift and pronoun shift works identically — see Backshift.
entries.transform: "I've arrived safely," she wrote. -> She wrote that she had arrived safely.
examples: He wrote that the apartment was smaller than the pictures suggested.
She wrote me twice from Lisbon and then went quiet.
Write to your representative if you feel strongly about it.
The critic wrote that the second act saves the play.
He wrote a long email explaining exactly what had gone wrong.
She never wrote back.
